planting.note: Direct sow in consistently moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; no scarification needed, but a light stratification improves uniformity. Keep soil evenly damp through establishment since this species naturally colonizes streambanks and wet meadow margins.

directions: Also called springbank clover, this western North American native spreads by rhizomes and stolons to form a low, mat-forming groundcover along streambanks, wet meadows, vernal pool margins, and coastal bluffs from British Columbia to Baja California and east into the Rockies. Rose-pink to purple-red clover heads bloom from spring into summer and draw a wide range of native bees; as a legume it also fixes nitrogen and improves disturbed riparian soils. Plant in full sun to light shade in consistently moist ground -- it tolerates seasonal flooding and some foot traffic, making it useful as a native lawn or meadow alternative in wetland restoration and hedgerow plantings. The rhizomes were historically harvested and cooked as a food source by several Pacific Coast Indigenous peoples.

planting.note: Fall-sow into gravelly, fast-draining soil in full sun so seed experiences natural winter cold-moist stratification; germination and flowering the following spring are slow but reliable once the taproot establishes.

directions: Native to dry sagebrush steppe, rocky slopes, and open oak woodlands of the interior Pacific Northwest, this clover produces unusually large flower heads -- up to two inches across, often bicolored pink-purple and cream -- that are disproportionately showy for its low, basal-rosette habit. Grow from a persistent woody taproot in lean, well-drained, rocky or gravelly soil in full sun; once established it is highly drought tolerant and resents heavy, wet, or amended garden soil. Its early-to-mid spring bloom provides an important nectar source for native bees emerging in dry steppe habitat before most other forbs flower. Best suited to rock gardens, dryland native plantings, and steppe restoration seed mixes rather than conventional borders.

planting.note: Scarify seeds and soak in warm water before direct sowing into dry to medium, well-drained soil in full sun; tolerates calcareous prairie soils typical of its native limestone-prairie habitat.

directions: A tall, sturdy taprooted legume of dry-mesic to dry tallgrass prairie and limestone glades from the Great Plains east through the Midwest, Illinois tick trefoil holds its dense, gray-green, pubescent trifoliate foliage in a strongly upright clump. Clusters of pink-purple pea-like flowers open in July and August, followed by the distinctive hooked, bur-like seed segments characteristic of the tick trefoils, which cling to fur and clothing for dispersal. As a nitrogen-fixing legume it thrives in lean, dry prairie soil where many showier perennials struggle, and its foliage serves as a larval host for silver-spotted skippers and other prairie skipper butterflies. Site in full sun in a restored or recreated prairie planting where its late-summer bloom fills a gap between early and fall-blooming prairie forbs.

planting.note: Scarify seeds and soak in warm water before direct sowing into average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; benefits from nearby shrubs or tall grasses to lean on as it matures.

directions: Found at woodland edges, clearings, and thickets across the eastern US, large tick trefoil is the biggest-podded member of its genus, with a sprawling, often leaning habit that can reach six feet or more when supported by surrounding vegetation. Pointed ('cuspidate') trifoliate leaflets back loose, airy racemes of small pink-purple pea flowers from midsummer into early fall, followed by unusually large hooked seed segments that readily cling to fur and fabric. Grow in full sun to light shade in average, well-drained soil at the edge of a woodland garden or shrub border rather than in an open, exposed site, since the lax stems benefit from nearby structure. Like other Desmodium species it fixes nitrogen and provides larval forage for several native skipper butterflies.

planting.note: Scarify seeds and soak in warm water before direct sowing into dry, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; a specialist for lean sand or gravel prairie sites rather than average garden loam.

directions: Named for its narrow, stalkless (sessile) leaflets that give the plant a finer, almost willow-like texture than most tick trefoils, this slender perennial is a specialist of dry sand prairies, sandy roadsides, and gravelly open ground across the central and eastern US. Small pink-purple pea flowers appear in loose terminal clusters from midsummer through early fall, followed by the characteristic hooked, segmented tick-trefoil pods. It performs best in lean, fast-draining sandy soil in full sun and is notably drought tolerant once its deep taproot is established, making it a good nitrogen-fixing companion for other sand-prairie natives like little bluestem and prairie sandreed. The foliage and flowers support prairie skipper butterflies and a range of small native bees.
